q: Sorry, I can't talk right now - I ___ in a meeting.
why: I always takes am. Be is the base form: it cannot be the finite verb straight after a subject, so it needs a modal or an imperative around it, as in You must be tired or Don't be late.
tn: Verb To Be (am / is / are, was / were)

q: ___ you at the office yesterday when the power went out?
why: You always takes were, even for one person, and yesterday rules out the present are.
tn: Verb To Be (am / is / are, was / were)

q: I ___ with you - the deadline is completely unrealistic.
why: Agree is a full verb and never needs be. This is the single most common be error.
tn: Verb To Be (am / is / are, was / were)

q: My brother ___ 30 next month.
why: English states age with be, not have, so He has 30 is impossible. Be also states a fixed future fact: He is 30 next month means the same as He will be 30 next month.
tn: Verb To Be (am / is / are, was / were)

q: Everyone ___ really helpful when we arrived at the hotel.
why: Everyone looks plural but takes a singular verb, so the past form is was.
tn: Verb To Be (am / is / are, was / were)

q: ___ this the right platform for the train to Ayutthaya?
why: This is singular, and be forms its own question by moving in front of the subject - no does.
tn: Verb To Be (am / is / are, was / were)

q: The film went on for three hours, so by the end I ___ .
why: The -ed form describes how you felt, and by the end places it in the past. Boring would describe the film, not you.
tn: Verb To Be (am / is / are, was / were)

q: She ___ want to join us - she said she's got plans.
why: Want is an action verb, so its negative uses doesn't. Be cannot make another verb negative.
tn: Verb To Be (am / is / are, was / were)

q: 'Are you coming to the party tonight?' 'Yes, I ___ .'
why: A short answer reuses the verb from the question: are you becomes I am.
tn: Verb To Be (am / is / are, was / were)

q: There ___ a couple of things I want to check before we ship this.
why: There agrees with the noun that follows it, and a couple of things is plural.
tn: Verb To Be (am / is / are, was / were)

q: It ___ raining hard when we left, so we got completely soaked.
why: It takes was in the past, and we left fixes the sentence in past time.
tn: Verb To Be (am / is / are, was / were)

q: We ___ not ready to launch - half the tests are still failing.
why: Are still failing shows the situation is happening now, so the present are is needed, not the past were.
tn: Verb To Be (am / is / are, was / were)

q: ___ your parents both from Bangkok originally?
why: Parents is plural and there is no past time reference, so the present plural are is correct.
tn: Verb To Be (am / is / are, was / were)

q: I ___ at home all evening, so it can't have been me you saw at the mall.
why: I takes was in the past, and the whole sentence is an argument about last night.
tn: Verb To Be (am / is / are, was / were)

q: I ___ wondering if you might have five minutes this afternoon.
why: Native speakers use the past I was wondering to sound polite and less demanding, even though the request is about right now. Been needs have in front of it, and were does not agree with I.
tn: Verb To Be (am / is / are, was / were)

q: My manager ___ every email within an hour, which honestly stresses me out.
why: My manager is a third-person singular subject, so the verb takes -s, and within an hour describes a habit rather than a single moment.

q: ___ you usually take the BTS or a taxi to work?
why: Usually signals a routine, and the subject you needs the auxiliary do; does belongs to he, she and it.

q: She ___ on Fridays - she does four long days instead.
why: Doesn't already carries the third-person -s, so the main verb after it stays in the base form work.

q: According to the timetable, the last train ___ at 12.05.
why: According to the timetable marks a fixed public schedule, and schedules take the simple present with the third-person -s.

q: I ___ what you mean, but the deadline still worries me.
why: Know is a state verb, so it stays simple even about this moment, and the subject I never takes -s.

q: I ___ my work email after nine at night.
why: An adverb of frequency sits directly before the main verb, and the subject I takes no -s.

q: First you ___ the garlic, then you add the chilli and stir for a minute.
why: Then you add in the second clause shows this is a recipe instruction, and instructions use the simple present base form.

q: Everyone on my team ___ from home on Wednesdays.
why: Everyone is grammatically singular despite meaning several people, and on Wednesdays makes it a weekly routine.

q: I usually ___ from home, but this week I'm in the office every day.
why: The contrast with this week I'm in the office proves the first clause is the long-term habit, so it takes the simple present.

q: What time ___ the pharmacy on the corner close on Sundays these days?
why: The pharmacy is third-person singular, and these days fixes the question in present time, so the auxiliary is does and not did.

q: 'Do you take card?' 'Yes, we ___ .'
why: A short answer repeats the auxiliary used in the question, so do you becomes we do.

q: My landlord ___ two other flats in the same building.
why: Have becomes has after a third-person singular subject, and ownership meanings avoid the continuous form.

q: I ___ eat beef, so could we choose somewhere else?
why: The subject I takes don't, and eat is a main verb, so it needs do-support rather than a form of be.

q: My sister ___ English at a school in Chiang Mai.
why: My sister is third-person singular, and verbs ending in -ch add -es, so teach becomes teaches.

q: How often ___ your colleagues work at the weekend?
why: Colleagues is plural, so the auxiliary is do, and how often shows we are asking about frequency.

q: Keep your voice down - the baby ___ in the next room.
why: Keep your voice down points at this exact moment, so the action in progress needs is sleeping.

q: Sorry, I can't come tonight. I ___ my parents from the airport at eight.
why: Tonight at eight describes an arrangement already fixed, and the continuous is how English states a definite plan.

q: ___ you working late again tonight?
why: Working is an -ing form, so the question opens with the auxiliary be, and you always takes are.

q: I ___ what you mean, but I still think the price is too high.
why: Understand is a stative verb about the mind, so it refuses the -ing form even when you mean right now.

q: My upstairs neighbour ___ moving furniture around at midnight.
why: The complaint pattern puts always between be and the -ing verb, giving is always moving.

q: These days more and more Thai companies ___ to a four day week.
why: These days plus more and more marks a trend in progress, and companies is plural, so are moving fits.

q: This soup ___ amazing. What's in it?
why: Taste used as a sense verb reports a quality rather than an activity, so the simple form tastes is standard.

q: Don't call her now - she ___ dinner with her family.
why: Now shows the meal is in progress, and have dinner is an action, so the continuous is allowed here.

q: He ___ his phone. He's probably still on the plane.
why: The second sentence shows the situation is happening now, and not sits between is and the -ing verb.

q: What time ___ tomorrow?
why: Tomorrow signals a fixed arrangement, and in a wh- question the auxiliary are must come before the subject you.

q: She normally works in Chiang Mai, but this month she ___ in the Bangkok office.
why: Normally works states the permanent habit, while this month marks the temporary change the continuous exists for.

q: I ___ of moving closer to the office - the commute is killing me.
why: Think of meaning consider is an active mental process, unlike think meaning believe, so the continuous works.

q: ___ they still arguing about the budget?
why: Still arguing shows an unfinished action, and the plural subject they forces the auxiliary are.

q: We can't use the big room - Nick and Priya ___ interviews in there until four.
why: Nick and Priya is a plural subject and the room is occupied right now, so are doing is the only fit.

q: She ___ for her IELTS test at the moment.
why: At the moment forces the continuous, and study keeps its y before -ing, so the spelling is studying.

q: I ___ to Japan three times, and I'd go again tomorrow.
why: Three times counts experience with no date attached, and been to means visited and returned.

q: We ___ the contract last Friday, so the work starts on Monday.
why: Last Friday is a finished time word, and a finished time word blocks the present perfect completely.

q: How long ___ for this company?
why: How long asks about a period reaching the present, and the auxiliary must come before you.

q: She's been off sick ___ Tuesday, so we split her workload.
why: Tuesday is the starting point of the absence rather than its length, and starting points take since.

q: I've had this laptop ___ about four years and it still runs fine.
why: About four years measures a length of time, and every length of time takes for.

q: I still ___ from the recruiter, and it's been two weeks.
why: Still plus a negative marks something expected that has not happened, which needs the present perfect.

q: Have you ever ___ to a rooftop bar in Bangkok?
why: Have you ever asks about life experience, so the verb after have must be the participle been.

q: The parcel ___ yet, so I'll chase the courier this afternoon.
why: Yet marks something expected but still missing, and after hasn't you need the participle arrived.

q: 'Where's Malee?' 'She ___ to the bank; she'll be back soon.'
why: She'll be back soon shows she is away right now, and gone to means away while been to means returned; have gone does not agree with she.

q: I ___ four cups of coffee today and it's only lunchtime.
why: Today is an unfinished period so the count is still open, and the participle of drink is drunk.

q: Everyone on the team ___ the new policy, so we can move on.
why: Everyone takes a singular verb, so the auxiliary is has, and so we can move on shows the result matters now.

q: This is the first time I ___ Thai food this spicy.
why: This is the first time is a fixed frame that always takes the present perfect, not a present simple.

q: When ___ the report? I need to know the exact date.
why: I need the exact date shows the question is about one finished moment, which rules out the present perfect.

q: So far this quarter we ___ four new clients.
why: So far this quarter names a period that has not ended, so the total is still open and can rise.

q: Big news: the client ___ the proposal.
why: Big news signals a fresh event, and just sits between has and the participle accepted.

q: She ___ in three different countries so far, so she settles in anywhere.
why: So far marks a period that is still open, which rules out the past simple, and the present second clause shows the experience explains what she is like now.

q: How many countries ___ so far?
why: So far means up to this point in your life, an open period, so the question needs have plus a participle.

q: I ___ her since 2019, and we still work on the same floor.
why: Since 2019 fixes an unfinished period, which forces the present perfect, and the participle is known.

q: All applicants ___ by email, so there is no need to call them.
why: Applicants receive the action rather than doing it, so the passive is needed, and the plural subject takes have been.

q: ___ many customers complained about the new checkout this week?
why: This week is not over yet, so the present perfect is right, and customers is plural so the auxiliary is Have.

q: I'm still stuck outside - I ___ for a taxi for half an hour.
why: Still stuck outside shows the wait is running right now, and for half an hour measures it, which is exactly what have been plus -ing is for.

q: You're covered in flour. ___ baking?
why: Covered in flour is present evidence of an activity that has only just stopped, which is the classic trigger for this tense.

q: I ___ three chapters of the report, so you can review those now.
why: So you can review those now points at a finished product, and three chapters is a counted result that takes the simple form.

q: We ___ each other since university.
why: Know is a state verb, so even with since university it stays in the simple form.

q: How long ___ on that proposal? You look shattered.
why: You look shattered is visible evidence of a recent, continuing activity, which is exactly what the present perfect continuous is for.

q: He looks awful - he ___ well since the move.
why: Since the move opens a period running up to the present, and he looks awful points at an ongoing pattern rather than one bad night.

q: You ___ that same excuse all week.
why: All week plus the note of irritation about a repeated action is where a native speaker chooses the active continuous; have been used is passive and cannot take that same excuse as its object.

q: I ___ with my cousin for the past month while my flat is being repaired.
why: For the past month and the clause about the flat mark a temporary arrangement that is still going on.

q: Sales ___ steadily since the campaign launched, which is encouraging.
why: Since the campaign launched leaves the period open, and steadily describes a trend still in progress.

q: How many emails ___ so far this morning?
why: How many asks for a completed number, so the counted result takes the simple form rather than the continuous one.

q: My manager ___ me to apply for the team lead role for months.
why: My manager is singular and therefore takes has, while for months fixes a period that reaches the present.

q: ___ you been feeling any better since you changed the medication?
why: Been feeling needs the auxiliary have, and the subject you never combines with has.

q: I ___ to reach you all afternoon yesterday, but your phone was off.
why: All afternoon yesterday closes the period, so the present perfect is impossible and the past continuous is correct.

q: The two departments ___ on a shared roadmap since March.
why: The two departments is plural and takes have, while since March keeps the period open up to now.

q: ___ about what you said, and I think you're right.
why: I've been thinking is the standard native opener for reflection that has continued up to this moment; I have think is not a possible form.

q: I ___ my laptop at the office yesterday and had to go back for it.
why: Yesterday fixes a finished time, so the past form left is required; have left cannot sit with a finished time marker.

q: Sorry, I ___ your message until this morning.
why: The auxiliary already carries the past, so the verb goes back to its base form see, and until this morning rules out the present.

q: ___ you speak to the landlord yesterday, or shall I call him?
why: Yesterday points to a finished conversation, and only did forms a past question with the base form speak.

q: I ___ live in Chiang Mai, but I moved to Bangkok for work.
why: Used to plus the base form live describes a past habit, and moved confirms the situation is over.

q: Who ___ out the meeting invite? Half the team never got it.
why: Who is the subject of the verb here, so English drops the auxiliary and uses the past form sent directly.

q: The company ___ its Bangkok office in 2019, long before I joined.
why: In 2019 is a closed year, which blocks the present perfect and forces the simple past opened.

q: We ___ dinner about an hour ago, so I'm not hungry.
why: Ago always points back to a finished moment, and the simple past had is the only form that fits it.

q: We ___ the offsite for October, but then the budget was cut.
why: Plan doubles its final n before -ed, and but then the budget was cut places the decision firmly in the past.

q: It ___ my idea at the time - Preecha suggested it in the first place.
why: At the time fixes the sentence in past time, and the verb is be, so its past negative is wasn't; didn't would need a main verb after it.

q: How much ___ for the flight in the end?
why: In the end closes the event off in finished past time, and a past wh- question puts did before the subject and keeps pay in its base form.

q: ___ you use to work weekends at your old company?
why: Use to only follows the auxiliary did in a question, and your old company shows the habit is finished.

q: She ___ the wrong charger, so my phone died in the meeting.
why: Bring is irregular and its past form is brought, and my phone died places the whole sentence in past time.

q: I got to the restaurant, ___ for twenty minutes, and then she texted to say she couldn't come.
why: Got and texted are both simple past forms in the same list, so the middle verb has to match them as waited.

q: My grandmother ___ born in a village near Ubon.
why: Born always needs a form of be, and a person's birth is a finished event, so was is the right choice.

q: As soon as the rain ___, we walked back to the hotel.
why: Walked back sets the sentence in past time, so the clause after as soon as also takes the past form stopped.

q: The repair ___ me three thousand baht, which felt steep.
why: Cost does not change its form in the past and never takes an -ed ending; felt shows the sentence is past.

q: 'Did you remember to book the meeting room?' 'Yes, I ___.'
why: A short answer reuses the auxiliary from the question, and the question here begins with Did.

q: In all the years I worked there, I ___ met the CEO.
why: Worked there shows the job is over, so the finished narrative takes the past never met rather than the present perfect.

q: I ___ to Japan twice in 2018, and I loved it both times.
why: Twice in 2018 counts specific finished occasions, and used to cannot express a set number of times.

q: How long ___ the visa application take in the end?
why: In the end signals a completed process and take is in its base form, so the auxiliary has to be did.

q: I ___ my emails when the fire drill started.
why: When the fire drill started is the short interrupting event, so the longer background action takes was plus checking.

q: We ___ for the delayed train for nearly two hours.
why: We takes were, and the verb after it must be the -ing form waiting.

q: I ___ exactly what she meant, but I decided to say nothing.
why: Know is a state verb, so it stays in the past simple even when the moment is ongoing.

q: ___ you doing when the delivery guy rang the bell?
why: You takes were, and in a direct question the auxiliary moves in front of the subject.

q: While I ___ the slides, Mai was rehearsing her introduction.
why: Was rehearsing in the second clause shows two actions running side by side, so both clauses take the past continuous.

q: I know it's short notice, so I ___ if you had a spare ticket.
why: The subject I takes was, and the past form was wondering is the standard polite softener before a favour.

q: When I walked into the office, everyone ___ at their phones in total silence.
why: Everyone takes a singular verb, and when I walked into the office is the point that cuts into the ongoing scene.

q: I was carrying two coffees when someone ___ straight into me.
why: The bump is the short, finished event inside the longer action, so it takes the past simple.

q: I ___ complaining - I was just explaining why the file was late.
why: The continuous negative puts not on the auxiliary, and was just explaining fixes both the tense and the subject.

q: My old flatmate was always ___ his dishes in the sink for me to find.
why: Always plus the past continuous describes a repeated, irritating habit, and the verb after was needs -ing.

q: She said she couldn't stay, because she ___ her sister at the airport at six.
why: At six points to a fixed arrangement she had already made, and English reports such plans with the past continuous.

q: At three o'clock yesterday afternoon I ___ in the dentist's chair.
why: At three o'clock yesterday afternoon names one exact moment, and we describe being in the middle of something at that moment with the continuous.

q: ___ we were driving through the tunnel, the radio cut out completely.
why: During is followed by a noun, not a clause, so as is what introduces the background action here.

q: 'Were the neighbours arguing again last night?' 'Yes, they ___.'
why: A short answer repeats the auxiliary from the question, and the plural neighbours takes were.

q: The insurance company asked what ___ at the time of the accident.
why: After asked what the question becomes reported, so the subject I comes before was doing and there is no inversion.

q: By the time we arrived, the caterers ___ everything away.
why: By the time we arrived marks a later past point, so the packing that finished before it takes had packed.

q: She told me she ___ the report the night before.
why: The original words were I finished the report last night, and after the past reporting verb told that past simple backshifts to the past perfect, with last night becoming the night before.

q: If I ___ about the train strike, I would have left an hour earlier.
why: Would have left in the main clause signals a third conditional, and its if-clause always takes the past perfect.

q: I ___ lunch already, so I just had a coffee with them.
why: Had must be followed by the participle eaten, and so I just had a coffee keeps the whole situation in the past.

q: After I had checked in, I ___ straight to the lounge.
why: Had checked already marks the earlier action, so the second, later action stays in the past simple.

q: I didn't reply to your message because I ___ it - it went straight into spam.
why: The message was still unseen before the past moment of not replying, so the negative past perfect shows which came first.

q: ___ you already left when the fire alarm went off?
why: Already left plus the past clause when the fire alarm went off needs a past perfect question, which starts with Had.

q: It was the first time she ___ presented to the board, and she was terrified.
why: It was the first time fixes the frame in the past, and this pattern always continues with had plus a participle.

q: By the time they called my number, I ___ in that queue for over an hour.
why: By the time they called puts everything earlier than that past point, and for over an hour adds the duration.

q: When the auditors asked for the file, I was relieved: I ___ a backup the night before.
why: The night before is earlier than the past moment when the auditors asked, so only had made shows the correct order.

q: ___ the reviews before I booked that hotel - the photos were ten years old.
why: Wish plus the past perfect is the standard pattern for regretting something you failed to do before a past event.

q: Which sentence means the meal was completely finished before the guests arrived?
o: When the guests arrived, we had eaten.
When the guests arrived, we ate.
When the guests arrived, we were eating.
When the guests arrived, we eat.
why: Only had eaten places the meal entirely before their arrival; the past simple ate would mean you started after they came in.

q: The flat was freezing when we walked in because the heating ___ off all week.
why: All week describes a state that ran up to the past moment we walked in, so the past perfect had been is required.

q: In the sentence "She'd already sent the money before I asked her to", what does 'd stand for?
why: The participle sent follows immediately, and only had joins a participle directly; if 'd were would, you would need have in between, as in she would have sent.

q: No sooner ___ the presentation than the projector died.
why: No sooner at the front of a clause forces inversion, so the auxiliary had moves in front of the subject.

q: I was exhausted by lunchtime because I ___ since five in the morning.
why: Since five in the morning measures a stretch running up to the past point by lunchtime, so had been driving is needed; have been driving would point at right now.

q: How long ___ you been waiting when the technician finally turned up?
why: Turned up fixes a past reference point, so the auxiliary must be had rather than the present-time have.

q: The pitch was cancelled because it ___ heavily all morning.
why: Was cancelled sets the story in the past and all morning stresses duration, so had been raining explains the result.

q: By the time she handed in her notice, she ___ at that agency for nine years.
why: By the time plus for nine years measures a period leading up to a past event, which is exactly what had been working expresses.

q: He ___ three emails before he realised he had the wrong address.
why: Three emails is a finished, countable result, so the simple had written fits; the continuous would stress the process instead.

q: We ___ each other for years before we ever worked on the same team.
why: Know is a stative verb and resists the -ing form, so the simple had known carries the duration here.

q: When I got home the kitchen was covered in flour, so I knew my flatmate ___ again.
why: I knew places the whole sentence in the past, and the flour is evidence of an activity in progress, so had been baking is the right form.

q: They ___ the road outside for weeks before anyone from the council came to check on the noise.
why: For weeks before anyone came marks an activity still in progress up to that past visit, so had been digging fits; had been dug is passive and cannot take the road as an object.

q: I'm shattered. I ___ on this proposal since eight this morning.
why: I'm shattered is present, so the period since eight this morning runs up to now and takes have been working, not the past form.

q: We ___ long before they called our table, maybe five minutes at most.
why: They called our table is a finished past event, so the wait is measured up to that past point with hadn't been waiting.

q: She was fed up because she ___ to fix the printer for half an hour and nobody had offered to help.
why: For half an hour explains the past state was fed up, so the cause takes the active had been trying, not the passive.

q: He told me he ___ for that promotion for two years, so the rejection really stung.
why: Told me backshifts the reported clause one step, turning have been pushing into had been pushing.

q: By nine o'clock the cleaners ___ the whole floor and had gone home.
why: The whole floor is a completed result and had gone home confirms the job was over, so the simple had finished is correct.

q: They'd been living out of suitcases ___ March, which is why the flat looked so bare.
why: March names a starting point rather than a length of time, so since is required with had been living.

q: The pipes ___ for months, which is why the ceiling eventually gave way.
why: The collapse is a past result and for months measures the activity behind it, so the active had been leaking is right.

q: 'The printer's jammed again.' 'Hang on, I ___ have a look at it.'
why: Hang on marks a reaction decided at this very moment, and an on-the-spot decision takes will.
tn: Simple Future: will and going to

q: We've already booked the venue, so we ___ launch the new range in October.
why: We've already booked shows the decision was taken before now, and an earlier decision is reported with going to.
tn: Simple Future: will and going to

q: Slow down and look at those clouds - it ___ pour down any minute now.
why: Look at those clouds gives visible evidence both speakers can see, and shared visible evidence selects going to.
tn: Simple Future: will and going to

q: I don't think they ___ the migration before Friday, but that is only my gut feeling.
why: I don't think plus a personal opinion with no evidence in the room is exactly where will belongs.
tn: Simple Future: will and going to

q: I can't do Wednesday afternoon - I ___ the dentist at four.
why: An appointment already fixed in your diary is normally announced with the present continuous, am seeing.
tn: Simple Future: will and going to

q: Send the invoice over tonight and I ___ it first thing tomorrow, I promise.
why: I promise marks a commitment made at the moment of speaking, and promises are made with will.
tn: Simple Future: will and going to

q: My laptop ___ connect to the hotel wifi, however many times I restart it.
why: Won't describes a machine that stubbornly refuses to work, which is the standard use of won't with objects.
tn: Simple Future: will and going to

q: Call me when you ___ at the airport and I'll come down to arrivals.
why: After the time word when, English keeps a present form even though arrive clearly points to the future.
tn: Simple Future: will and going to

q: Those bags look really heavy. ___ carry one up for you?
why: The standard way to offer help on the spot starts with Shall, and the heavy bags show the offer is spontaneous.
tn: Simple Future: will and going to

q: ___ you going to apply for the team lead role, or are you happy where you are?
why: Going to takes a form of be as its auxiliary, and the subject you requires are, never do or will.
tn: Simple Future: will and going to

q: Passengers ___ be notified by text message of any change of departure gate.
why: Formal notices to the public prefer will, which sounds official and impersonal rather than personally planned.
tn: Simple Future: will and going to

q: ___ a shuttle bus from the hotel to the conference centre on Sunday?
why: A question about future existence inverts to Will there be, keeping there directly after will.
tn: Simple Future: will and going to

q: ___ you let me know as soon as the shipment clears customs, please?
why: Will you plus please is a direct request aimed at a person, not a prediction about the future.
tn: Simple Future: will and going to

q: I ___ a bit late tonight - the meeting before mine always overruns.
why: Probably sits between will and the main verb, so will probably be is the standard order in a prediction.
tn: Simple Future: will and going to

q: Ask Malee about the expenses system - she ___ know exactly what to do.
why: Will here expresses a confident assumption about what someone already knows, and know is a state verb, so will be knowing is not possible.
tn: Simple Future: will and going to

q: This time on Sunday we ___ over the Andaman Sea.
why: This time on Sunday names a moment when the flight is already in progress, and the pattern is will + be + the -ing form.

q: ___ the car this evening, or can I take it to the gym?
why: The speaker is checking a plan the other person already has rather than asking for a decision, and do you use would ask about a habit.

q: Text me when you ___ and I'll be waiting right outside arrivals.
why: After when English uses a present form for future meaning, so land is correct even though the whole sentence is about later.

q: The recruiter said I ___ by Friday whether I got the job.
why: Know describes a state, not an activity in progress, so it stays out of the continuous even with a future time marker.

q: The team ___ the migration by Friday, so Monday should be quiet.
why: By Friday sets a deadline for completion rather than a moment in the middle of the work, so the future perfect beats the continuous here.

q: I ___ the standup tomorrow - I'll be on a plane at nine.
why: The second clause puts the speaker mid-flight at standup time, and the negative keeps the frame won't + be + the -ing form.

q: Nok ___ the new dashboard at the all-hands on Friday.
why: The third person changes nothing in this pattern, so will be presenting is used for she exactly as it is for I and they.

q: What ___ this time next year?
why: In a wh- question will jumps in front of the subject while be keeps its place, which gives what will you be doing.

q: Leave the report with me - I ___ late anyway, so it's no trouble.
why: Anyway shows the late night is already part of the plan, and that scheduled flow is exactly what will be working expresses.
