q: ___ the traffic was terrible, we still got there before the doors opened.
why: The gap is followed by the full clause the traffic was terrible, so only the conjunction even though fits; the other three need a noun.

q: The match was called off ___ the storm warning.
why: The storm warning is a noun phrase with no verb in it, which forces because of rather than the conjunction because.

q: Despite ___ twice, she still has not had a reply from the landlord.
why: Despite is a preposition, so it needs a noun or an -ing form. She emailed and she has emailed are clauses, and the bare verb email cannot follow a preposition here, so emailing is the only fit.

q: ___ the noise from the building site, I slept surprisingly well.
why: In spite of is fixed and cannot lose of, despite never gains one, and the noise is a noun, so although is impossible here.

q: The invoice was sent on Monday. ___, the client says he never received it.
why: The full stop closes the first sentence, so the link must be an adverb that can open a new one; however is the only option that can.

q: My laptop died halfway through the demo, ___ I had to finish on my phone.
why: A comma joining a result clause needs the conjunction so; therefore is an adverb and would demand a semicolon or a new sentence.

q: You are writing a formal project report. Which sentence is correct?
o: The costs rose sharply, therefore we paused the rollout.
The costs rose sharply, therefore, we paused the rollout.
Because of the costs rose sharply, we paused the rollout.
The costs rose sharply; therefore, we paused the rollout.
why: Therefore is an adverb, so the two clauses need a semicolon or a full stop between them and a comma after therefore.

q: Although he apologised, ___.
why: Although already marks the contrast, so adding but or however repeats it; English allows only one connector between the two clauses.

q: We got the project over the line ___ having only three developers.
why: Having is an -ing form rather than a clause, and the small team is an obstacle, not the reason for success, which rules out because of.

q: 'The flat is a bit small.' 'It is cheap, ___.'
why: Only though can sit at the end of a sentence as a spoken afterthought. Although and even though must open a clause, and despite must be followed by a noun or an -ing phrase.

q: The first two attempts failed. ___, the team kept going and shipped on Friday.
why: The gap starts a new sentence and points back to the failures, so the contrast adverb nevertheless is needed; the rest cannot stand before a comma alone.

q: We ate at the hotel ___ everything else in town was fully booked.
why: The second clause gives the reason for eating at the hotel, so because is right; so would turn the full restaurants into the result.

q: ___ the fact that we had been warned, nobody backed up the database.
why: Despite the fact that is the fixed way to put a clause after a preposition; in spite would need of, and because of reverses the logic.

q: You are texting a friend about a film you did not enjoy. Which reply is correct and natural?
o: Despite the reviews were great, I was bored senseless.
Although the reviews were great, but I was bored senseless.
The reviews were great, but I was bored senseless.
Nevertheless the great reviews, I was bored senseless.
why: Only this option uses one connector correctly: despite cannot take a clause, although cannot pair with but, and nevertheless cannot take a noun phrase.

q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Although we booked months ago the seats were terrible.
Although, we booked months ago, the seats were terrible.
Although we booked months ago, the seats were terrible.
Although we booked months ago. The seats were terrible.
why: A concession clause placed first closes with a comma before the main clause, takes no comma after although, and cannot stand as its own sentence.

q: The car's making a strange noise again, so I'm going to ___ this weekend.
why: The garage does the work, so serviced comes after the object it and never before it.
tn: Causative: have and get something done

q: We got the whole ceiling ___ over the long weekend, so the place still smells of paint.
why: The office receives the action, so a past participle is required after the object.
tn: Causative: have and get something done

q: Don't worry about the client deck. I'll have Priya ___ it before the call.
why: Have plus a named person is followed by the bare verb, with no to and no third person s.
tn: Causative: have and get something done

q: The wording is too technical for me. Can you get someone in legal ___ it before it goes out?
why: Get plus a person takes to before the verb, and that is the main difference from have.
tn: Causative: have and get something done

q: He ___ on the metro in Paris, and his residence card was inside it.
why: The second clause shows he was the victim, so the wallet must sit before the participle.
tn: Causative: have and get something done

q: I can't make the nine o'clock standup tomorrow, because I ___ my eyes tested at half eight.
why: Tomorrow makes this a fixed future arrangement, so the continuous form of have is the one that fits.
tn: Causative: have and get something done

q: Our landlord still ___ the boiler fixed, and we reported it three weeks ago.
why: Still plus a complaint that continues now points to the present perfect, so the participle had follows.
tn: Causative: have and get something done

q: The photocopier has jammed again. Shall I ___ before the meeting?
o: have someone to look at it
why: A person follows have directly, and the verb after that person keeps its base form.
tn: Causative: have and get something done

q: I don't cut my own hair, so I ___ every six weeks at the place by the office.
why: The first clause says somebody else does the work, so the object goes in front of cut.
tn: Causative: have and get something done

q: They ___ twice in the same month, so they have finally installed cameras.
why: The cameras show they were the victims, so the shop belongs between had and the participle.
tn: Causative: have and get something done

q: You should ___ before the rainy season starts.
why: A roof cannot do the checking, so it comes first and the past participle follows it.
tn: Causative: have and get something done

q: This invoice has the wrong company name on it, so I'll ___ it reissued this afternoon.
why: Have is the causative that takes an object plus a past participle. Let takes a bare infinitive, do is not a causative verb at all, and make works with a participle only in fixed phrases such as make yourself understood.
tn: Causative: have and get something done

q: The training room needs setting up. Can you ___ before lunch?
why: Facilities is the team doing the work, so the bare verb do follows the name of that team.
tn: Causative: have and get something done

q: ___ your car serviced yet, or is it still making that noise?
why: Yet points to the present perfect, and the past participle of have is had.
tn: Causative: have and get something done

q: Applicants who studied outside the country must ___ their transcripts translated by a certified translator.
why: Must is followed by a bare verb, and have is the verb that works with an object plus a participle.
tn: Causative: have and get something done

q: ___ the report at two in the morning, she went straight to bed.
why: Having plus the past participle marks the earlier of two actions, and the object the report blocks any passive reading.

q: The people ___ outside the clinic have been there since seven.
why: The main verb have been already carries the tense, so the blank takes the participle rather than a second finite verb.

q: Please ignore the invoice ___ yesterday; the amount on it is wrong.
why: The invoice receives the action, so the reduced relative uses the passive participle with no form of be.

q: Having read your proposal carefully, ___
o: a few points are still unclear.
I still have a couple of questions.
there are two things to clarify.
why: The hidden subject of the reading is a person, so only the version beginning with I keeps the two subjects the same.

q: ___ the only person in the office with a car, I got asked to do the airport run.
why: A clause in front of the comma must open with a participle, and the meaning here is active, so the -ing form Being is required. Been needs having in front of it, Be and To be are not participles at all.

q: Before ___ anything, run it past legal.
why: Before works as a preposition here, so the verb that follows it takes the -ing form.

q: ___ by three different reviewers, the paper was accepted without changes.
why: The phrase by three different reviewers shows the paper received the action, so the passive participle opens the clause.

q: Guests ___ after eleven at night should use the side entrance.
why: Guests do the arriving, so the active -ing form is what reduces the relative clause after the noun.

q: ___ what to do next, I emailed the project manager.
why: The negative word goes in front of the participle, and the -ing form gives the active meaning the sentence needs.

q: Once ___, the form cannot be edited by the applicant.
why: The form receives the action, so once is followed by the passive participle with the subject and be left out.

q: ___ that the client is joining at ten, we need the deck finished by nine.
why: This is the fixed participle phrase used to introduce a fact both sides already accept, here the ten o'clock start.

q: ___ the terms of your policy, we are unable to issue a refund on this booking.
why: The reviewing happened before the refusal and we did it, so the perfect active participle is the only fit.

q: The engineer ___ the demo tomorrow has done this a hundred times.
why: Tomorrow rules out a past form, and the sentence already has its main verb, so the blank needs the -ing form.

q: ___ by the sudden drop in orders, management called an emergency meeting.
why: The by-phrase shows management received the shock rather than causing it, so the passive participle is correct.

q: Which sentence keeps the participle clause attached to the right subject?
o: Having missed the train, the meeting started without me.
Having missed the train, I joined the call from the platform.
Having missed the train, my seat was given away.
Having missed the train, the taxi took nearly an hour.
why: Only that version makes the person who missed the train the subject of the main clause, which is what the structure demands.

q: It was Ploy ___ found the double booking, not the finance team.
why: The focus Ploy is a person and is the subject of the clause that follows, so who is the link; whom would only fit an object.

q: It was the humidity ___ finished me off, not the heat.
why: For a non-human focus the link word is that, or more formally which; who is impossible because the humidity is not a person, what never links an it-cleft, and which it leaves a redundant subject pronoun.

q: ___ I need most right now is a clear brief, not another meeting.
why: A wh-cleft opens with What, which serves as the subject of the whole sentence and the object of need at the same time.

q: ___ I want is a straight answer about the refund.
why: All introduces the relative clause I want by itself, so nothing may be added between it and the subject.

q: ___ we cancelled the trip was that my passport was still at the embassy.
why: The subject slot needs a noun phrase headed by reason, which the reason why gives you. Because opens an adverbial clause and cannot be a subject, the reason of must be followed by a noun rather than a clause, and why the reason is not a possible phrase.

q: I know it looks like I forgot, but I ___ the invoice on Monday.
why: Emphatic do contradicts the listener, and forgot plus on Monday places the action in finished past time.

q: She may not say much in meetings, but she ___ care about getting the details right, and she always has.
why: And she always has keeps the sentence in present time, so the emphatic auxiliary stays present, and she takes the third person form does.

q: What the team ___ was rewrite the whole onboarding flow in a weekend.
why: The bare infinitive rewrite after was needs a matching past do-clause, and in a weekend describes a finished job.

q: The design ___ live with; the timeline I cannot.
why: Fronting moves the object to the front but leaves subject and verb in normal order, so the subject comes before the modal.

q: Never before ___ such a strong response to a job advert.
why: The fronted negative adverb never before pulls the auxiliary in front of the subject in the clause that follows.

q: 'Was it the airline that lost your bag?' 'No, ___ - the airline was fine.'
o: it the hotel that lost it
it was the hotel what lost it
was it the hotel that lost it
it was the hotel that lost it
why: The reply is a statement answering No, so the subject it comes before was and the two halves join with that.

q: What I'd really like ___ me a copy of the signed contract before Friday.
why: The focus after is has its own subject you, and English introduces such a subject with for plus a to-infinitive.

q: It isn't the workload ___ me, it's the constant switching between projects.
why: The focus the workload is a thing, and the second half needs its own verb, so the contracted that is form fits.

q: The reason ___ the trial was stopped is set out in section four.
why: After the noun reason, why introduces the clause that explains it; because of has to be followed by a noun, not a clause.

q: ___ was that the client changed the brief two days before delivery.
why: What happened works as the subject of the sentence and sets up the explanation that follows the linking verb.

q: We're still waiting on the client's ___ before we can start development.
why: The possessive client's must be followed by a noun, and the noun built from approve is approval.

q: Don't bother arguing with him. He's completely ___ once he's made up his mind.
why: Flexible takes the negative prefix in-, and the other three prefixes never combine with this root.

q: We ordered 5,000 units and sold barely 400, so we clearly ___ demand.
why: Ordering far more than you sell shows the estimate was too high, which is exactly what over- signals here.

q: Half the team left in March and nobody was hired, so the department is badly ___.
why: Losing half the team means there are too few people, so under- plus the past participle is right.

q: I ___ the deadline as the 15th when the client had actually said the 5th.
why: Mis- carries the meaning of wrongly, so misread describes reading something and getting it wrong.

q: The ___ of the brief saved us a whole week of back and forth.
why: The slot after the article needs a noun, and the noun that goes with clear in this sense is clarity.

q: Everything in the report is ___ from public sources, so nothing there is confidential.
why: The gap describes a property of the information, so it needs an adjective, and -able on verify gives verifiable, meaning able to be checked. Verification is a noun, verify a verb and verifying a participle.

q: The training was expensive but surprisingly ___ - our error rate halved in a month.
why: The adverb surprisingly modifies an adjective, so the -ive form effective is the one that fits.

q: He's been off work for a month, and everyone's been really ___ about covering his shifts - I haven't had to ask anyone twice.
why: Covering his shifts is a positive act, so the -ful adjective is right; the -less form means unable to act.

q: Complaining to the front desk turned out to be ___ - absolutely nothing changed.
why: The clause nothing changed shows the complaint had no effect, which the suffix -less expresses.

q: The two sides finally reached an ___ after nearly three hours of arguing.
why: The article before the gap forces a countable noun, and the noun from agree is agreement.

q: The excuse he gave was completely ___ to the actual complaint.
why: Relevant begins with r, and the prefix in- changes to ir- in front of that letter.

q: Please ___ my last email; I sent it to the wrong thread by accident.
why: Dis- reverses the verb regard and gives disregard, meaning to ignore something deliberately.

q: The junior analyst presented the figures ___ and the whole board was impressed.
why: The gap says how the analyst presented the figures, so it needs the -ly adverb confidently; confident and confidential are adjectives and confidence is the noun.

q: What struck me about the hotel staff was their ___ to help with absolutely anything.
why: The possessive their calls for a noun, and -ness turns the adjective willing into one.

q: The verb compete carries its main stress on the second syllable. In the noun competition, the main stress falls on ___.
why: The suffix -tion pulls the main stress onto the syllable immediately before it, giving compeTItion.

q: Her report was full of ___, which made the conclusions very hard to trust.
why: Full of takes a noun, and the plural of the negative noun is what fits after that phrase.

q: He always says two days and it always takes a week, so he really does ___.
why: Promising less time than the work takes means promising too much, which is the sense of over-.

q: The lack of ___ between the two teams is causing a lot of duplicated work.
why: The lack of must be followed by a noun, and communication is the noun in this family.

q: Both dates are ___ for me, so just pick whichever one suits the client.
why: The gap follows the verb are and describes the dates, so an adjective ending in -able is needed.

q: I finally replaced my laptop bag with ___ tote I found in Chiang Mai.
why: Size comes before colour and colour before material, so small, then black, then canvas. Canvas says what the tote is made of, so it touches the noun.

q: Tense and awkward are both opinion adjectives. Which version is punctuated correctly?
o: It was a tense, and awkward conversation.
It was a tense, awkward conversation.
It was an awkward, tense, conversation.
It was a tense awkward, conversation.
why: Two adjectives of the same kind take one comma between them and nothing at all before the noun conversation.

q: We've just signed ___ contract with the supplier in Penang.
why: A compound modifier in front of a noun takes a hyphen and keeps year singular, even though the deal itself runs for three years.

q: The keynote was given by ___ consultant who flew in from Singapore.
why: An adverb ending in -ly already attaches to the adjective after it, so standard English leaves highly and paid unhyphenated.

q: He's on ___ probation period, so let's not pile work on him yet.
why: The number and the noun join with a hyphen, month stays singular inside the modifier, and the phrase still needs its article.

q: ___ weeks of the sprint were chaotic, but we pulled it back after that.
why: Ordinal numbers come in front of cardinal numbers, so first sits before two. Thai and French speakers often reverse this pair.

q: He turned up to the pitch in ___ suit that clearly cost more than my car.
why: Gorgeous is an opinion so it leads, colour follows, and origin sits closest to the noun. Italian tells us where the suit was made, not what the speaker thinks of it.

q: We inherited ___ table that takes up half the kitchen.
why: Size comes before age and material comes last, so huge, then old, then oak. Oak names the material and has to touch the noun.

q: The gift shop was full of ___ bowls that cost almost nothing.
why: Origin comes before material, so Thai goes in front of ceramic, and size opens the string because it is the least specific of the three.

q: She keeps ___ machine in the spare room and never touches it.
why: Opinion first, then origin, then the purpose word. Sewing says what the machine is for, so nothing can come between sewing and machine.

q: Which version would a copy editor leave untouched in a supplier report?
o: We need a reliable, low cost supplier based in Vietnam.
We need a reliable low-cost, supplier based in Vietnam.
We need a reliable, low-costs supplier based in Vietnam.
We need a reliable, low-cost supplier based in Vietnam.
why: Reliable and low-cost are coordinate here, since you could reverse them or join them with and, so a comma goes between them; low-cost is one hyphenated modifier that never takes a plural s, and no comma ever separates the last modifier from its noun.

q: It's ___ walk from the station, so take a taxi if the rain keeps up.
why: Minute stays singular inside a hyphenated modifier. The plural only appears when you say that the walk takes ten minutes.

q: The documentary opens with drone footage of ___ shark off the Queensland coast.
why: The hyphen ties man and eating into a single modifier describing the shark. Man-eaten reverses who eats whom, and the other two are not possible compound forms.

q: Pack ___ boots; the last hour of the trail is steep and loose.
why: Walking says what the boots are for, so it sits next to the noun, and the determiner those has to open the whole phrase.

q: It isn't in this jacket. Try ___, the one hanging by the door.
why: Other belongs with the determiner my and comes before any describing word, so black follows it rather than leading the phrase.

q: Before the company moved to Rama IX, I ___ walk to the office in ten minutes, but now the commute takes an hour.
why: But now marks a finished past routine. Of these four options only used to can be followed by the base verb walk: the be used to forms would need walking after them, and use to is simply the wrong spelling here.
tn: Used To / Be Used To / Get Used To

q: Don't worry about the noise on the call - I ___ working in an open-plan office.
why: Don't worry places this in the present, and the -ing form working needs be plus the full phrase before it.
tn: Used To / Be Used To / Get Used To

q: The first week of night shifts was brutal, but I'm slowly ___ sleeping during the day.
why: Slowly points to a process that is still going on, which is exactly what the get form in a continuous tense expresses.
tn: Used To / Be Used To / Get Used To

q: He ___ take criticism well, but two years of coaching have changed that completely.
why: Have changed shows the habit is over, and the auxiliary did already marks the past, so the verb keeps its base spelling.
tn: Used To / Be Used To / Get Used To

q: Every summer my grandfather ___ drive us down to Hua Hin in his old pickup.
why: Every summer describes a repeated past action, and would takes a bare base verb with nothing between them.
tn: Used To / Be Used To / Get Used To

q: When we were kids we ___ a dog called Bobby, though I barely remember him.
why: Having a dog is a state rather than a repeated action, so the past habit form fits here and would does not.
tn: Used To / Be Used To / Get Used To

q: After ten years in Bangkok, she's completely ___ the traffic.
why: She's supplies the verb be, so the familiarity phrase follows with its final -d and links straight to the noun.
tn: Used To / Be Used To / Get Used To

q: I ___ hate public speaking, but after two years of client demos I actually enjoy it now.
why: I enjoy it now contrasts with a feeling that has ended, so the finished past habit form plus the base verb hate is needed.
tn: Used To / Be Used To / Get Used To

q: It took me months to get used to ___ in English all day.
why: The to in get used to is a preposition, so the verb after it appears in its -ing form.
tn: Used To / Be Used To / Get Used To

q: ___ you use to work at the Sathorn branch, or was that your brother?
why: The base form use to in the stem is the version that appears in questions about finished past habits, and it needs the auxiliary did.
tn: Used To / Be Used To / Get Used To

q: Managers here are used to ___ challenged in meetings; nobody takes it personally.
why: In are used to, the word to is a preposition rather than part of an infinitive, so the verb after it must take the -ing form - here the passive being challenged.
tn: Used To / Be Used To / Get Used To

q: These days I ___ waking up before my alarm; my body just does it.
why: These days fixes the sentence in the present, so a past form would clash with the current routine being described.
tn: Used To / Be Used To / Get Used To

q: We ___ to Krabi three times when I was at university.
why: Three times counts a definite number of trips, and habit forms describe unspecified repetition rather than a fixed total.
tn: Used To / Be Used To / Get Used To

q: Sorry if I sound blunt on calls - I ___ speaking English every day.
why: The speaker is explaining a present difficulty, and speaking after the phrase requires the be form with its final -d.
tn: Used To / Be Used To / Get Used To

q: There ___ be a coffee shop on this corner, but it closed during the pandemic.
why: It closed shows the shop no longer exists, and the past habit form is what carries a bare infinitive like be.
tn: Used To / Be Used To / Get Used To

q: The ground is wet, so it ___ rained during the night.
why: Wet ground is strong evidence, so must have shows a confident deduction.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: I ___ told her the secret. Now she is angry with me.
why: The action happened and was a mistake, so shouldn't have shows regret.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: He only left five minutes ago, so he ___ arrived yet.
why: Can't have expresses a confident negative deduction about something impossible so soon.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: We ___ the earlier flight, but we decided to sleep in.
why: Could have plus the past participle taken describes an unused past possibility.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: She ___ my email, because she never replies this slowly.
why: The word not goes directly after the modal and before have.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: Which sentence is written correctly?
why: Only the past participle gone is possible after should have in writing.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: You ___ me you were coming, and I would have cooked something.
why: Should have told criticises a past action that did not happen.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: The lights are off, so they ___ home already.
why: Have never changes to has after a modal verb like must.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: I ___ that joke at the meeting. Everyone went quiet.
why: The joke happened and was a mistake, so shouldn't have made fits.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: In fast natural speech, should have usually sounds like ___.
why: The weak have collapses into a very short sound written as shoulda.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: He ___ been waiting outside for an hour. He looks frozen.
why: Looking frozen is evidence, so must have marks a confident past deduction.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: That ___ been Anna at the door, because she is in Bangkok today.
why: Can't have rejects the idea as impossible given the clear evidence.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: I ___ you last night, but my phone battery died.
why: Would have plus called shows a past intention blocked by a problem.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: Applicants ___ their documents before the deadline, but many did not.
why: Should have submitted criticises applicants for not completing a past duty.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: What does might have plus a past participle usually express?
o: a definite fact about the future
an uncertain guess about the past
why: Might have signals that the speaker is unsure about a past event.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: The road was closed, so the driver ___ another route.
why: Only could have plus the participle taken is grammatically correct here.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: You ___ so rude to the waiter. He was only doing his job.
why: Be becomes been after have, and shouldn't have expresses clear criticism.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: Nobody answered the phone, so they ___ already gone to lunch.
why: Might have plus gone offers a possible explanation for the silence.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: Which sentence shows a confident negative deduction about the past?
o: She can't have finished the exam so quickly.
She shouldn't have finished the exam.
She might not have finished the exam.
She could not finish the exam yesterday.
why: Can't have expresses certainty that something was simply not possible.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: We ___ the hotel earlier, because now everything is fully booked.
why: Should have booked shows regret about a past action we did not take.
tn: Modal Perfect: should have / must have / could have / might have

q: You ___ to wear a helmet on this site.
why: Be supposed to needs the verb be plus the written d on supposed.
tn: Be Supposed To / Be Meant To / Be Due To

q: The plane ___ to land at eleven, but fog delayed it.
why: The subject is singular and the correct past phrase is was due to.
tn: Be Supposed To / Be Meant To / Be Due To

q: This tool ___ to cut plastic, not metal.
why: Purpose and design are expressed with be meant to plus a base verb.
tn: Be Supposed To / Be Meant To / Be Due To

q: We ___ supposed to use our phones during the exam.
why: The negative attaches to the verb be, so we say are not.
tn: Be Supposed To / Be Meant To / Be Due To

q: I was supposed to send the email yesterday. What does this usually mean?
why: The past form usually tells us the planned action did not happen.
tn: Be Supposed To / Be Meant To / Be Due To

q: How ___ I supposed to finish this by Friday?
why: Be supposed to uses the verb be, so this question needs am.
tn: Be Supposed To / Be Meant To / Be Due To

q: The results ___ to be announced on Monday morning.
why: A plural subject takes are, and due to introduces the scheduled event.
tn: Be Supposed To / Be Meant To / Be Due To

q: You're ___ to knock before you come in.
why: The written form always keeps the d, even though nobody pronounces it.
tn: Be Supposed To / Be Meant To / Be Due To

q: ___ we supposed to bring our own laptops?
why: Questions with supposed to invert the verb be with the subject.
tn: Be Supposed To / Be Meant To / Be Due To

q: The meeting was ___ to start at nine, but the room was locked.
why: Was due to describes a timetable, and only due fits this pattern.
tn: Be Supposed To / Be Meant To / Be Due To

q: Which sentence talks about the purpose of a design?
o: The bus is due to leave soon.
This lamp is meant to save energy.
You are supposed to queue here.
She was supposed to phone me.
why: Be meant to points at the purpose the designer had in mind.
tn: Be Supposed To / Be Meant To / Be Due To

q: My visa ___ to expire next month, so I need to renew it.
why: A fixed future date on a document takes is due to plus a verb.
tn: Be Supposed To / Be Meant To / Be Due To

q: He ___ supposed to tell anyone about the surprise.
why: The past negative puts the word not directly after the verb was.
tn: Be Supposed To / Be Meant To / Be Due To

q: In fast speech, the phrase supposed to usually sounds like ___.
why: The d and the t join together into one quick sound.
tn: Be Supposed To / Be Meant To / Be Due To

q: Which sentence uses 'be supposed to' correctly?
why: A plural subject needs were, the written d, and the word to.
tn: Be Supposed To / Be Meant To / Be Due To

q: Quick, the bus ___ leave!
why: About to needs the verb be and the word to.
tn: Be About To / Be Going To / Was Going To

q: I ___ to call you, but my phone died.
why: Was going to shows a past plan that never happened.
tn: Be About To / Be Going To / Was Going To

q: She is on the point of ___ her job.
why: On the point of is always followed by an -ing form.
tn: Be About To / Be Going To / Was Going To

q: We ___ meet at six, but the meeting was cancelled.
why: We takes were, and the changed plan needs going to.
tn: Be About To / Be Going To / Was Going To

q: Which sentence shows a plan that did not happen?
o: I am going to buy it tomorrow.
I was going to buy it, but it sold out.
I am about to buy it.
I will buy it if I can.
why: Only the past form was going to signals a cancelled plan.
tn: Be About To / Be Going To / Was Going To

q: Do not phone him now. He ___ give a presentation.
why: The presentation starts in seconds, so is about to fits here.
tn: Be About To / Be Going To / Was Going To

q: The plane ___ take off. Please fasten your seat belt.
why: A take-off in seconds needs the present form is about to.
tn: Be About To / Be Going To / Was Going To

q: I was ___ about to send the email when you walked in.
why: Just before about to means the action almost started.
tn: Be About To / Be Going To / Was Going To

q: ___ you going to tell her the truth?
why: Questions with going to use the verb be at the front.
tn: Be About To / Be Going To / Was Going To

q: They ___ going to move to Chiang Mai, but they changed their minds.
why: They needs were, and the plan changed, so the past wins.
tn: Be About To / Be Going To / Was Going To

q: Look at those clouds. It ___ rain.
why: Present evidence like clouds points forward, so is going to fits.
tn: Be About To / Be Going To / Was Going To

q: Which sentence correctly describes a plan that changed?
o: We are going to drive, but we took the train.
We was going to drive, but we took the train.
We were going to drive, but we took the train.
We were go to drive, but we took the train.
why: Were going to plus a contrast clause shows the plan changed.
tn: Be About To / Be Going To / Was Going To

q: The results ___ published in ten minutes.
why: Results is plural and the verb needs a passive be after to.
tn: Be About To / Be Going To / Was Going To

q: He ___ apply for the visa last month, but he lost his passport.
why: Last month plus a failed plan needs was going to here.
tn: Be About To / Be Going To / Was Going To

q: I ___ leaving when the phone rang.
why: The fixed expression is on the point of, never in the point of.
tn: Be About To / Be Going To / Was Going To

q: We ___ better hurry or we will miss the train.
why: Only had combines with better to make this warning structure.
tn: Had Better / Would Rather / May As Well / It's Time

q: I'd rather ___ at home this evening than go out.
why: When the subject stays the same, would rather takes a bare infinitive with no to. A new subject after it takes the past simple instead, as in I'd rather you told me.
tn: Had Better / Would Rather / May As Well / It's Time

q: You had better ___ late for the interview.
why: In the negative, not goes directly after better and before the verb.
tn: Had Better / Would Rather / May As Well / It's Time

q: It's time we ___ seriously about the budget.
why: After it is time plus a subject, the verb takes the past simple form.
tn: Had Better / Would Rather / May As Well / It's Time

q: Everything is closed, so we ___ as well go home.
why: The fixed expression is may as well or might as well, nothing else.
tn: Had Better / Would Rather / May As Well / It's Time

q: I'd rather you ___ me the truth now.
why: When a different subject follows would rather, we use the past simple.
tn: Had Better / Would Rather / May As Well / It's Time

q: Which sentence gives the strongest warning?
o: You had better see a doctor.
why: Had better carries a bad result, so it is stronger than should.
tn: Had Better / Would Rather / May As Well / It's Time

q: She would rather work from home ___ commute for two hours.
why: The second option after would rather is introduced by than.
tn: Had Better / Would Rather / May As Well / It's Time

q: ___ you rather have tea or coffee?
why: Questions with rather begin with would, because would rather is fixed.
tn: Had Better / Would Rather / May As Well / It's Time

q: It is time the company ___ its safety rules.
why: The past simple after it is time still describes the present situation.
tn: Had Better / Would Rather / May As Well / It's Time

q: Which is the correct negative of had better?
why: Had better forms its negative by adding not after better.
tn: Had Better / Would Rather / May As Well / It's Time

q: We ___ prefer to receive your reply by email.
why: Would prefer is the polite formal pattern followed by to plus infinitive.
tn: Had Better / Would Rather / May As Well / It's Time

q: We are already at the airport, so we ___ check in now.
why: May as well fits because there is no better option right now.
tn: Had Better / Would Rather / May As Well / It's Time

q: I would rather ___ the film at home than pay for a ticket.
why: The bare infinitive follows rather when the subject stays the same.
tn: Had Better / Would Rather / May As Well / It's Time

q: You had better ___ your ticket before you board.
why: Had better takes the base form of the verb with no ending.
tn: Had Better / Would Rather / May As Well / It's Time

q: I wish I ___ more free time during the week.
why: Wish about an unreal present situation takes the past simple form.
tn: Wish / If Only / Hope and As If / As Though

q: I ___ the parcel arrives before Friday, because the client needs it.
why: The delivery is still genuinely possible, so hope is the natural verb.
tn: Wish / If Only / Hope and As If / As Though

q: I wish I ___ that email before the meeting started.
why: Regret about a finished past action needs wish plus the past perfect.
tn: Wish / If Only / Hope and As If / As Though

q: I wish my colleague ___ answering my messages so late.
why: A complaint about somebody's repeated behaviour uses wish plus would.
tn: Wish / If Only / Hope and As If / As Though

q: If only we ___ the traffic report before leaving home.
why: If only about a past mistake requires had plus a past participle.
tn: Wish / If Only / Hope and As If / As Though

q: He behaves as if he ___ the most experienced person here.
why: An unreal comparison after as if prefers the past subjunctive were.
tn: Wish / If Only / Hope and As If / As Though

q: I wish I ___ speak in meetings without feeling nervous.
why: Can must shift back to could after wish in unreal present statements.
tn: Wish / If Only / Hope and As If / As Though

q: Which sentence correctly expresses a possible future event?
o: I wish you pass the exam tomorrow.
I hope you pass the exam tomorrow.
I wish you passed the exam tomorrow.
I hope you passed the exam tomorrow.
why: A real future possibility takes hope plus a present tense verb.
tn: Wish / If Only / Hope and As If / As Though

q: It ___ as though the printer has broken down again.
why: The subject it needs the third person singular form looks here.
tn: Wish / If Only / Hope and As If / As Though

q: She spends money as though she ___ a millionaire.
why: Were signals that the comparison is clearly unreal and imagined.
tn: Wish / If Only / Hope and As If / As Though

q: We wish the office ___ closer to a train station.
why: Wish about an unreal present fact takes were for all subjects.
tn: Wish / If Only / Hope and As If / As Though

q: I wish they ___ me about the schedule change earlier.
why: The change already happened, so the past perfect shows past regret.
tn: Wish / If Only / Hope and As If / As Though

q: ___ I had listened to my teacher back then.
why: If only introduces a strong regret about an earlier past action.
tn: Wish / If Only / Hope and As If / As Though

q: I ___ we can meet for dinner when you visit next month.
why: The dinner is a realistic future plan, so hope fits naturally.
tn: Wish / If Only / Hope and As If / As Though

q: You sounded as if you ___ this film several times already.
why: Had watched pushes the impression one step back into the past.
tn: Wish / If Only / Hope and As If / As Though

q: The film was ___ boring that we left after twenty minutes.
why: So goes before a bare adjective like boring with no noun.
tn: Degree and Result: so/such...that, too...to, enough...to

q: It was ___ a long flight that I could not sleep at all.
why: Such is needed before the noun phrase a long flight.
tn: Degree and Result: so/such...that, too...to, enough...to

q: This suitcase is ___ heavy to carry up the stairs.
why: Too plus adjective plus infinitive shows the action is blocked.
tn: Degree and Result: so/such...that, too...to, enough...to

q: She is not old ___ to drive a car in this country.
why: Enough always comes after the adjective old, never before it.
tn: Degree and Result: so/such...that, too...to, enough...to

q: We do not have ___ for everyone in the room.
why: Enough comes before a noun, so enough chairs is the natural order.
tn: Degree and Result: so/such...that, too...to, enough...to

q: Which sentence means you cannot drink the soup right now?
why: Too signals a problem, while very hot soup is simply enjoyable.
tn: Degree and Result: so/such...that, too...to, enough...to

q: He spoke ___ quickly that nobody understood him.
why: So also works before adverbs such as quickly in this pattern.
tn: Degree and Result: so/such...that, too...to, enough...to

q: They were ___ kind people that we stayed an extra night.
why: Such appears before plural nouns with no article in front.
tn: Degree and Result: so/such...that, too...to, enough...to

q: The water is warm ___ for swimming this morning.
why: After the adjective warm, enough is the only correct position.
tn: Degree and Result: so/such...that, too...to, enough...to

q: I was too tired ___ dinner last night.
why: Too plus an adjective is followed by the infinitive with to.
tn: Degree and Result: so/such...that, too...to, enough...to

q: The bus was so full ___ we waited for the next one.
why: The result clause after so plus adjective begins with that.
tn: Degree and Result: so/such...that, too...to, enough...to

q: This coat is ___ small for me. I need a bigger size.
why: Too small means the coat cannot be worn, which fits here.
tn: Degree and Result: so/such...that, too...to, enough...to

q: It was ___ an expensive hotel that we only stayed one night.
why: Such is used before a noun phrase starting with an.
tn: Degree and Result: so/such...that, too...to, enough...to

q: There was ___ noise that I could not hear the announcement.
why: Noise is uncountable, so so much is the correct choice.
tn: Degree and Result: so/such...that, too...to, enough...to

q: Which sentence uses 'enough' in the right position?
o: He is enough tall to reach it.
He is tall enough to reach it.
He is too tall to reach it enough.
He is such tall that he reaches it.
why: Enough follows adjectives, giving us tall enough to reach it.
tn: Degree and Result: so/such...that, too...to, enough...to

q: ___, I already sent the invoice yesterday.
why: Actually corrects a wrong belief that the invoice was never sent.

q: A: Can you finish by six? B: ___, I will try but I cannot promise.
why: Well softens an answer that is not a clear yes.

q: ___, where did you park the car?
why: By the way introduces a small new topic that just occurred to you.

q: We were interrupted, so ___, the report needs two more days.
why: As I was saying resumes a point after an interruption stopped you.

q: It costs fifty baht, ___ fifteen, sorry.
why: I mean repairs a word that you have just said incorrectly.

q: ___, that is enough about work; tell me your news.
why: Anyway closes the current topic and moves the conversation forward.

q: The train leaves in two minutes. ___, we have to leave now or we miss it.
why: Look adds urgency and pushes the listener to act immediately.

q: Which marker is the most suitable choice in a formal business meeting?
why: In fact carries the same idea but suits formal spoken English.

q: ___, shall we begin with the first item?
why: So opens a new stage of the talk and starts the business.

q: A: The train leaves at nine. B: ___, it leaves at eight thirty.
why: Actually politely corrects the wrong time the other speaker gave.

q: ___, I have never been to Japan before.
why: You know softens a personal disclosure and checks that the listener is still following you. It does not ask the listener for information.

q: Where does a discourse marker most often sit in a sentence?
o: Between an auxiliary and a main verb
At the start of a clause
Between an article and a noun
why: Markers normally stand at the front, marked off by a short pause.

q: ___, so the exam is on Monday morning.
why: Right confirms shared information and signals that you are ready.

q: Which reply sounds least rude when you disagree with a colleague?
why: Well delays the disagreement and softens the blow for your listener.

q: ___, the results confirm the original hypothesis.
why: In fact adds supporting evidence and fits an academic presentation well.

q: Sorry, that was a long digression. ___, could I ask one more question about the contract?
why: Anyway closes a digression and steers the conversation back to the main business, which is exactly what the first sentence sets up.

q: In fast speech, I do not know usually sounds like ___.
why: The three words squeeze together into one short unstressed chunk.

q: Why is a short filler often better than a long silence?
o: It makes your grammar correct automatically.
It replaces the main verb of the sentence.
It shows you are still thinking and holding your turn.
It shortens the conversation for the listener.
why: Silence suggests you have finished or that you disagree with them.

q: ___, what I meant was that the flight was cheaper.
why: I mean opens a clearer explanation of your own earlier words.

q: Which marker best returns you to the main point after a long side story?
why: Anyway signals the end of the digression and resumes the topic.

q: The food was ___ salty, but I still ate everything.
why: A bit is the fixed softener before an adjective in this sentence.

q: I ___ like the new office, but the journey is long.
why: Kind of goes directly before the main verb with no be verb.

q: Let's meet at ___ and decide from there.
why: The suffix -ish attaches to the end of the number, written eight-ish or eightish. It never stands alone in front of the word.

q: There were ___ thirty guests at the small ceremony.
why: Around comes straight before a number with no extra preposition attached.

q: We could watch a film ___ tonight if you are free.
why: Or something softens a suggestion in positive statements, unlike or anything.

q: She studies history, art ___ at university.
why: The fixed vague phrase is and stuff like that with uncountable stuff.

q: Which sentence sounds most polite to a manager?
o: There seems to be a small issue with the plan.
The plan is bad and you know it.
why: There seems to be softens criticism and protects the working relationship well.

q: I ___ we should book the tickets soon, before prices rise.
why: I guess is a present hedge introducing a soft opinion or suggestion.

q: The presentation was ___ long, but the content was excellent.
why: Somewhat works before an adjective and fits a neutral or formal tone.

q: ___ we could try a different supplier next quarter.
why: Maybe is one word as an adverb starting a softened suggestion here.

q: Which sentence uses a bit correctly?
o: The cake is a bit wonderful.
The cake is a bit dry.
The cake is a bit of dry.
why: A bit pairs with negative adjectives like dry, not positive ones.

q: The repair will cost ___ five thousand baht in total.
why: Roughly is the adverb form used before an approximate number here.

q: I'm ___ sure the shop closes at nine on Sundays.
why: Not quite sure is the natural hedge showing partial certainty in English.

q: Which reply softens a refusal best?
o: I'm not sure I can make it, sorry.
why: Hedging with not sure keeps the refusal warm and saves face.

q: We would need ___ three weeks to complete the audit.
why: Approximately is the formal adverb used before a number in reports.

q: Do you live near the office? Yes, I ___.
why: The question uses do, so the short answer repeats do.

q: Has your flight landed? No, it ___ yet.
why: Has in the question means the short answer must use has.

q: I hate early meetings. ___ do I.
why: So plus auxiliary plus subject agrees with a positive statement.

q: She has never eaten durian, and ___ have I.
why: Neither agrees with a negative statement and inverts the auxiliary.

q: These cups are dirty. Please bring the clean ___.
why: Cups is plural, so the plural substitute ones is required here.

q: I do not want the heavy bag; I prefer the light ___.
why: Bag is singular and countable, so one replaces it correctly.

q: Guests who wish to check in early may ___ at the front desk.
why: Do so is the formal substitute for a repeated action.

q: Would you like to join us for lunch? I would love ___.
why: After love, the repeated verb is dropped and only to remains.

q: ___ a minute? I need to ask you something.
why: In fast speech, have you disappears and got opens the question.

q: ___ good, let's meet at seven.
why: The subject it is dropped, but the verb still keeps its s.

q: Did you remember to send the invoice? No, I ___.
why: The question used did, so the negative short answer uses did.

q: Are they still waiting outside? Yes, they ___.
why: Are in the question means the answer must repeat are.

q: I was told to wait, so I ___.
why: Did replaces the repeated verb waited in the second clause.

q: He can drive, but his sister ___.
why: The contrast keeps only the modal, and the main verb disappears.

q: Which shoes are yours? The black ___ by the door.
why: Shoes is plural, so ones stands in for the noun.

q: In fast speech, going to often sounds like ___.
why: Going to reduces to gonna before a base verb in casual speech.

q: Which sentence is correct in writing?
why: The reduced sound copies of, but only have is grammatically correct here.

q: She ___ to leave early today.
why: Third person singular needs wants, so wanna is impossible here.

q: The word of in a lot of people usually sounds like ___.
why: Of is a weak form and reduces to a very short unstressed sound.

q: Which sentence would suit a formal written report?
o: We are going to review the data.
why: Reduced spellings belong to speech, while formal writing keeps full forms.

q: In natural speech, I have got to go often sounds like ___.
why: Have got to compresses into gotta in relaxed everyday conversation.

q: Which word normally keeps its full strong sound in a sentence?
why: Content words like coffee carry stress, while function words reduce.

q: In fish and chips, the word and usually sounds like ___.
why: And reduces to a single n sound between two stressed nouns.

q: Which sentence is correct when written out in full?
o: Do you wanna me to help?
Do you want me to help?
why: Wanna cannot form when an object comes between want and to.

q: When can is unstressed, it usually sounds like ___.
why: Positive can weakens to a short unstressed syllable in normal speech.

q: How can you usually tell can't from can in speech?
why: Can't keeps a full stressed vowel while can shrinks to a weak one.

q: In next day, the letter t is often ___.
why: A t between two consonants commonly disappears in rapid speech.

q: In tell her, the h in her is usually ___.
why: The h in pronouns like her often drops after a consonant sound.

q: In pick it up, the three words usually link as ___.
why: Final consonants move forward into the next word's vowel sound.

q: Which is the correct written form of the spoken sound wudda?
why: Modal perfect always takes have, whatever the spoken sound suggests.

q: I ___ going to explain the process now.
why: The subject I always takes am, even when speech shortens it.

q: In casual speech, want to often merges into ___.
why: Want to merges into the standard informal spelling wanna.

q: Which sentence shows correct written English?
why: Third person needs has to, since gotta suits I and you in speech.

q: Why do learners often miss the word to when listening?
why: Function words lose stress, so they become short and almost invisible.

q: The best way to train your ear for reductions is ___.
why: Repeating real audio builds the sound patterns that reading alone cannot.

q: My brother ___ in a bakery near our house.
why: A singular subject in the present simple needs the -s ending.

q: There ___ three emails waiting in your inbox.
why: After there, the verb agrees with the plural noun emails.

q: Each of the students ___ a free notebook.
why: Each is always singular, so the verb takes the -s ending.

q: The box of old letters ___ under my bed.
why: The subject is box, a singular noun, not the plural letters.

q: The news ___ better this morning, luckily.
why: News looks plural but takes a singular verb in English.

q: Most of the cake ___ already gone.
why: After most of, the verb follows cake, which is singular.

q: Neither of my sisters ___ how to drive.
why: Neither takes a singular verb even before a plural noun.

q: Everybody in the office ___ the new manager.
why: Everybody is a singular word, so the verb needs -s.

q: My parents ___ dinner together every evening.
why: A plural subject takes the base verb with no -s.

q: Ten minutes ___ long enough for a short break.
why: A period of time counts as one single unit here.

q: The company ___ new staff every January.
why: Company is a singular subject here, so the verb takes -s. Are recruit and recruiting are not finite verbs and cannot stand alone after the subject.

q: Where ___ the keys to the front door?
why: The subject keys is plural, so the question uses are.

q: Physics ___ a lot of mathematics.
why: Physics ends in -s but behaves as a singular noun.

q: One of my friends ___ in London.
why: The subject is one, so the verb stays singular here.

q: There ___ a lot of traffic this morning.
why: Traffic is uncountable and singular, so is fits here.

q: The number of complaints ___ falling steadily.
why: The subject is number, which stays singular in this phrase.

q: My friend and I ___ to the gym on Tuesdays.
why: Two subjects joined by and make one plural subject.

q: None of the shops ___ open on the holiday.
why: None of plus a plural noun normally takes a plural verb in everyday English. Be is the base form and cannot be the finite verb on its own.

q: Everything in these bags ___ mine.
why: Everything is singular, so it needs the singular verb is.

q: How much ___ the tickets cost in total?
why: Tickets is plural, so the auxiliary in the question is do.

q: ___ shoes over there are mine, not the black ones.
why: The noun is plural and far away, so those is the correct choice.

q: There is ___ in the fridge, so we have to go shopping.
why: The verb is positive, so the negative meaning must sit in nothing.

q: ___ of my sisters live in Bangkok and love it there.
why: Only both takes the plural verb live when two people are meant.

q: Nobody helped me, so I carried all the boxes ___.
why: By myself is the fixed phrase that means with no help at all.

q: My best friend and I have known ___ since high school.
why: Two people knowing the other person needs the reciprocal phrase each other.

q: Neither of the two options ___ perfect for our small team.
why: Neither of takes a singular verb in careful and exam English.

q: ___ of the guests has arrived yet, so the room is empty.
why: None of works before the plus a noun and means zero people.

q: She hurt ___ badly while she was running in the park.
why: The subject and the object are the same person, so use herself.

q: ___ called while you were out, but she did not leave a name.
why: A positive statement about one unknown person needs someone as the subject.

q: I could not find my keys ___, and I looked in every room.
why: After the negative verb could not, English uses the any word anywhere.

q: You can take ___ bus, because they both go to the airport.
why: Either plus a singular noun means one or the other of two.

q: ___ is my colleague Nina, who joined our team last month.
why: English uses this to introduce a person who is standing near you.

q: The children made breakfast ___ while their parents were sleeping.
why: The plural reflexive form is themselves, and the other three are not English.

q: ___ of the information in that email was useful to us.
why: Information is uncountable, so only none of fits before it here.

q: ___ hurt themselves during the long training session on Friday.
why: A positive verb with a negative meaning about people needs nobody.

q: Which sentence joins the two clauses correctly?
o: I was tired, I went to bed early.
I was tired so, I went to bed early.
I was tired, so I went to bed early.
I was tired; so, I went to bed early.
why: A comma plus so correctly joins two complete sentences here.

q: ___ raining hard, so we stayed inside.
why: It's is the short form of it is, which this sentence needs.

q: The ___ office is on the second floor.
why: One manager owns the office, so we use apostrophe plus s.

q: All the ___ bags were left in the hall.
why: Many students own the bags, so the apostrophe follows the s.

q: We were late. ___ the film had not started.
why: A linking adverb starting a sentence takes a comma after it.

q: My brother, ___ lives in Osaka, is visiting us.
why: Who refers to people, and that cannot introduce a clause set off by commas. Which is for things, and whose shows possession.

q: Which sentence needs commas around the relative clause?
o: The man who fixed my laptop was very kind.
The people that helped us were students.
Mr Chen who fixed my laptop was very kind.
The bag that I bought is red.
why: Mr Chen is already identified, so the clause is extra information.

q: Which one is a complete sentence?
o: The office was closed on Monday.
why: It has a subject and a finite verb, so it stands alone.

q: In the sentence 'we study english every monday', how many words need a capital letter?
o: Two: the first word and English
Three: the first word, English and Monday
None: the sentence is already correct
why: The sentence needs three capitals: the first word of any sentence, the language English, and the day Monday. Languages and days are proper nouns, so they keep their capital letter wherever they appear in a sentence.

q: She likes swimming, running, and ___.
why: Every item in the list must use the same ing form.

q: Which sentence is a run-on?
o: I called her twice, but she did not answer.
I called her twice she did not answer.
I called her twice; she did not answer.
I called her twice. She did not answer.
why: Two complete sentences are pushed together with no punctuation at all.

q: ___ jacket is this?
why: Whose asks about the owner, while who's means who is.

q: We sold two hundred ___ last week.
why: A simple plural never needs an apostrophe before or after the s.

q: ___ I checked the report twice before sending it.
o: After I had finished the meeting with the client,
After I had finished the meeting with the client
After, I had finished the meeting with the client
After I had finished the meeting with the client;
why: A long introductory clause is normally followed by a comma before the main clause. After a short phrase such as After lunch the comma is optional.

q: The laptop is broken; ___ screen is cracked.
why: Its without an apostrophe shows possession, exactly like his or her.

q: 1985 is normally said as ___.
why: Years before two thousand split into two two-digit halves when spoken.
tn: Numbers, Dates, Times, Prices and Measurements

q: 2006 is usually said as ___.
why: Years in that first decade take two thousand plus the number.
tn: Numbers, Dates, Times, Prices and Measurements

q: The year 2026 is most often said as ___.
why: From twenty ten onwards speakers usually split the year into two pairs.
tn: Numbers, Dates, Times, Prices and Measurements

q: 7:15 is said as ___.
why: Fifteen minutes after the hour is quarter past that hour.
tn: Numbers, Dates, Times, Prices and Measurements

q: 8:50 is said as ___.
why: After the half hour English counts the minutes to the next hour.
tn: Numbers, Dates, Times, Prices and Measurements

q: In British English, 5 June is spoken as ___.
why: British speakers use the ordinal with of before the month name.
tn: Numbers, Dates, Times, Prices and Measurements

q: In American English, June 5 is usually spoken as ___.
why: American speakers put the month first and use an ordinal number.
tn: Numbers, Dates, Times, Prices and Measurements

q: A price of 12.99 pounds is normally said as ___.
why: Prices are said as two plain numbers with the currency word dropped.
tn: Numbers, Dates, Times, Prices and Measurements

q: Which sentence writes the compound measurement correctly?
o: It is a three-hour flight to Seoul.
It is a three-hours flight to Seoul.
It is a three hour's flight to Seoul.
It is a three hours flight to Seoul.
why: The unit stays singular and hyphenated when it describes the noun.
tn: Numbers, Dates, Times, Prices and Measurements

q: The number 0.75 is read aloud as ___.
why: Digits after a decimal point are read one at a time.
tn: Numbers, Dates, Times, Prices and Measurements

q: The fraction 2/3 is said as ___.
